newsitem.title: USA: Democrats say Hong Kong money swung 1994 election.
newsitem.headline: Democrats say Hong Kong money swung 1994 election.

text.p: Former Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour on Thursday told a probe into campaign finance abuse he had never done anything improper in an election campaign and said accusations against him were phony.

Barbour told the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee a $2.1 million loan guarantee to a Republican think tank in 1994, touted by Democrats as evidence the Republicans used foreign-raised funds, was perfectly legal.

Democrats, on the defensive over charges they illegally received foreign money during last year's campaigns, said the money, put up by a Taiwanese national, helped swing the 1994 elections when Republicans won control of Congress.
The $2.1 million from the Hong Kong-based Taiwanese Ambrous Young arrived in October 1994 at the think tank and $1.5 million of it went straight into Republican coffers days before the elections.

Barbour said he did not know the money came from Hong Kong until earlier this year but that fact made no difference to the legality of the transaction. He said the money was not used in campaigns and played no role in Republican victories.

Barbour said he was testifying to "refute the inaccurate, incomplete, misleading, misinterpreted and outright false claims ... and frankly to put the lie to some infuriatingly phony charges which are aimed at me personally."

Republicans have argued that the transaction was perfectly legal since the think tank, called the National Policy Forum, was not, like political parties, barred from receiving foreign funds and was heavily in debt to the Republican Party.

New Jersey Democratic Sen. Robert Torricelli told the hearing earlier: "The influence on the elections of the United States is clear. Our national debate was changed ... It was foreign influence on the elections of the United States."

Fred Volcansek, a Republican fund raiser who engineered the $2.1 million loan guarantee from Young, told the committee the money had arrived in October 1994, days before elections in which Republicans gained control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years.

The moment the money arrived, $1.5 million of it was transferred to Republican election committees across the nation. The Democrats released a list of 16 state Republican parties which received payments and said the Republicans picked up 26 seats in the House of Representatives and six Senate seats in those states.

Torricelli quoted from documents suggesting that Young had renounced his dual U.S. citizenship, apparently for tax reasons, shortly before transferring the funds and Volcansek agreed that he and other top Republicans had known this.
"It is arguable that the individual who had the largest impact of the 1994 elections was a foreign national who renounced U.S. citizenship potentially for tax purposes," Torricelli said.
Other documents show that Barbour always intended to use the money for the election campaign.
The National Policy Forum later defaulted on the loan and Young wound up losing $700,000.
The session was marked by numerous testy exchanges between Republicans and Democrats.

New Mexico Republican Pete Domenici said Democrats had been trying to strike oil in a dry well. "They have no case ... To suggest that this was a major influence on the last campaign ... it is an absurdity," he said.
Volcansek accused Democrats of conducting an unwarranted investigation into his affairs going back to 1989 in an effort to find incriminating data.

He testified that he recently became aware the Commerce Department had issued a worldwide bulletin requesting information about him from all places he visited as a department official from 1989 to 1992.
